title: Tithi
wikitext:
{{short description|Lunar day in the Hindu calendar}} {{for|the film|Thithi (film)|Astronomical basis of the Hindu calendar}} {{italic title}} {{More citations needed|date=July 2010}} [[File:Tithi.ogv|thumb|The astronomical basis of the Hindu lunar day]] In [[Vedic timekeeping]], a '''''tithi''''' is a "duration of two faces of moon that is observed from earth", known as ''milа̄lyа̄'' ({{langx|new|𑐩𑐶𑐮𑐵𑐮𑑂𑐫𑐵𑑅, मिलाल्याः}}) in [[Newar language|Nepal Bhasa]],{{cite web |last=Kapali|first=Rukshana |title=नेपाल संवत् - नेपाल सम्बत |url=https://nepalsambat.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/NBlearning_NSpages.pdf |website=Nepal Sambat |access-date=3 November 2021 |archive-date=3 November 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211103064346/https://nepalsambat.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/NBlearning_NSpages.pdf |url-status=dead}} or the time it takes for the [[ecliptic coordinate system|longitudinal]] [[angle]] between the [[Moon]] and the [[Sun]] to increase by 12[[degree (angle)|°]]. In other words, a tithi is a time duration between the consecutive epochs that correspond to when the longitudinal angle between the Sun and the Moon is an integer multiple of 12°. Tithis begin at varying times of day and vary in duration approximately from 19 to 26 [[hour]]s.{{cite book |last1=Defouw|first1=Hart |last2=Svoboda|first2=Robert |title=Light on Life: An Introduction to the Astrology of India |url=https://archive.org/details/lightonlife00hart |url-access=registration |quote=Shukla paksha -inpublisher:icon. |year=2003 |publisher=[[Lotus Press]] |isbn=0-940985-69-1 |page=[https://archive.org/details/lightonlife00hart/page/186 186]}} Every day of a [[lunar month]] is called tithi. == Duration and variability == A tithi is defined as the time taken for the longitudinal angle between the Sun and the Moon to increase by 12[[degree (angle)|°]]. While the average duration is approximately 23 hours 37 minutes, actual tithi lengths vary from about 19 hours, 59 minutes to 26 hours, 47 minutes depending on the Moon’s elliptical orbit and variable speed in the [[ecliptic]].This variation is a result of the Moon’s non-uniform motion as described in Indian astronomical treatises such as the [[Surya Siddhanta|Surya Siddhānta]] and confirmed through modern astronomical observations.{{Cite journal |last=Pingree |first=David |title=The Mesopotamian Origin of Early Indian Mathematical Astronomy |url=https://doi.org/10.1177/002182867300400102 |journal=Journal for the History of Astronomy |date=1973 |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=1–12 |doi=10.1177/002182867300400102 |bibcode=1973JHA.....4....1P |issn=0021-8286|url-access=subscription }} == Calculation methods: traditional vs modern == Traditional Panchāngas often compute tithi boundaries using mean motions of the Sun and Moon as given in the Sūrya Siddhānta and later siddhāntic texts. These methods produce approximate times for tithi transitions. In contrast, modern almanacs generated by astronomical institutions use true longitudes derived from high-precision ephemerides (e.g., NASA JPL DE series).These differences in calculation can result in discrepancies of several minutes, and in rare cases, up to an hour, between traditional and modern Panchāngas.{{Cite journal |last1=Narayanan |first1=Anil |last2=Oak |first2=Nilesh |date=2023-05-17 |title=Planetary nodes and apses in the Sūrya-Siddhānta |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s43539-023-00083-3 |journal=Indian Journal of History of Science |volume=58 |issue=2 |pages=87–95 |doi=10.1007/s43539-023-00083-3 |issn=0019-5235|url-access=subscription }}{{Cite journal |last=Kumar |first=Ajit |date=2018 |title=Information seeking behaviour of nehru memorial museum & library (NMML), New Delhi readers: A case study |journal=Library Herald |volume=56 |issue=3 |pages=368 |doi=10.5958/0976-2469.2018.00034.9 |issn=0024-2292|doi-access=free }} == Panchanga == [[File:Tithi Calculation.jpg|thumb|image to understand the calculation of tithi]]{{Hinduism}} A Hindu ''[[muhurta]]'' (forty-eight minute duration) can be represented in five attributes of Hindu astronomy namely, ''[[weekday|vara]]'' the weekday, ''tithi'', ''[[nakshatra]]'' the Moon's asterism, ''[[yoga]]'' the angular relationship between the Sun and Moon and ''karana'' half of tithi.{{cn|date=June 2026}} ''Tithi'' plays an important role along with ''nakshatra'' in Hindus' daily as well as special activities in selecting the ''muhurta''. There are auspicious ''tithis'' as well as inauspicious ''tithis'', each considered more propitious for some purposes than for other.{{Cite journal |last=Roy |first=Raja Ram Mohan |date=2019-07-01 |title=Sidereal Ecliptic Coordinate System of Sūryasiddhānta |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.16943/ijhs/2019/v54i2/49658 |journal=Indian Journal of History of Science |volume=54 |issue=2 |doi=10.16943/ijhs/2019/v54i2/49658 |issn=0019-5235}} In ''amānta'' lunar calendars, ''tithi''s are counted beginning at ''śukla pratipada'', while in the ''pūrṇimānta'' lunar calendars, ''tithi''s are counted from ''kr̥ṣṇa pratipada''. The ''śukla'' ''tithi''s are when the moon waxes, and the ''kr̥ṣṇa tithi''s are when the moon wanes. The average ''tithi'' lasts 23 hours 37.5 minutes, and can range from 19 hours 59 minutes to 26 hours 47 minutes. The calculation of ''tithi'' timings may also differ on whether one uses the traditional methods for calculating the Sun and Moon's movement as promulgated in the [[Surya Siddhanta|''Sūrya Siddhānta'']] or modern methods which correctly calculate the true motions of the Sun and Moon. The ''tithi'' in place at sunrise is considered the "''tithi'' of the day", although the ''tithi'' may end before the next sunrise in which case the next ''tithi'' begins. Because the length of a ''tithi'' is also variable a case can arise where a ''tithi'' begins after sunrise and ends prior to the next sunrise, which is called a ''kṣaya tithi''. The opposite phenomenon can occur where a ''tithi'' in place during a sunrise is still present in the following sunrise which is called an ''adhika'' or ''ahorātra tithi''.{{Sfn|Chatterjee|Chakravarty|p=295-298}} There are 30 ''tithis'' in each [[lunar month]], named as:{{Cite book |last1=Chatterjee |first1=S.
